OpenH1 logo board, round 3

One direction, eight ways: H1 as plausible military sci-fi. Five variants are field equipment (a hull marking, a patch, a serial plate, hazard blocks, an ID tag); three render the same marks the way 2001 console hardware would (backlit gunmetal, translucent jelly, chrome).

All lettering is a stencil alphabet drawn for this project, not a font: every stroke that would meet another is cut loose by a bridge. No eagle, globe, wings or star, no series lettering, and no X, orb or ring. Files are in website/logo/round3/, made by website/logo/round3/build.py. Rounds 1 and 2 are in logo-board.html and logo-board-2.html.

01

Field: stencil on an armour panel

Hull Marking

H1 sprayed through a stencil onto an armour panel: seams, four fasteners, chipped paint, a small serial and a signal-orange tab. It reads as a marking on real equipment rather than a logo.

Why it's safe. Our own stencil letters on a generic chamfered panel. No emblem, insignia, unit name or lettering from the series.

Why it's not UNSC or Xbox. Not UNSC: no eagle, globe, wings or star, and none of its type. Not Xbox: olive and sand, no X, orb or green.

02

Field: embroidered unit patch

Squad Patch

H1 embroidered in satin thread on an olive morale patch, with a merrowed edge, a running stitch and the name in orange: the badge a squad would sew on. As an app icon it sits on cloth.

Why it's safe. A plain rounded patch with our own letters; no unit, rank or service insignia of any real or fictional force.

Why it's not UNSC or Xbox. Not UNSC: no eagle, globe or wings, no rank devices from the series. Not Xbox: olive and tan thread, no X or orb.

03

Field: stamped equipment plate

Serial Plate

The ID plate riveted to a piece of kit: brushed aluminium, four screws, OPENH1 stamped on top, the unit number H1-001 in big stencil with the number in orange, and a data strip. The lockup is the plate itself.

Why it's safe. A generic equipment plate with our own name and number on it; no real or fictional maker, service or unit is named.

Why it's not UNSC or Xbox. Not UNSC: no emblem, crest or service name. Not Xbox: bare aluminium and orange, no X, orb or green.

04

Field: blocky stencil and hazard stripes

Hazard Block

H1 cut from heavy stencil blocks in black on safety yellow, above a band of hazard striping: the marking on a blast door or a loading bay. Blunt, loud and readable from across a hangar or a tab bar.

Why it's safe. Hazard striping is a universal safety convention, and the letters are our own stencil blocks.

Why it's not UNSC or Xbox. Not UNSC: no emblem, insignia or series lettering. Not Xbox: yellow and black, no X, orb or green.

05

Field: embossed identity tag

ID Tag

An identity tag pressed from steel: a raised H1, the name and two numbers embossed beside it, a rolled edge and a slot for the chain. Quiet and personal, the mark every member of the squad carries.

Why it's safe. A plain rounded tag with our own name and numbers; no real or fictional service, person or record.

Why it's not UNSC or Xbox. Not UNSC: no emblem or service details from the series. Not Xbox: bare steel, no X, orb or green.

06

2001 hardware: gunmetal, lit through the stencil

Backlit

The stencil cut through a gunmetal console panel, with lime light shining through the letters and a power pip glowing below, as if the hardware has just switched on. Military marking, 2001 hardware.

Why it's safe. A rounded metal panel and our own stencil letters lit from behind; nothing from the game's equipment, interface or type.

Why it's not UNSC or Xbox. Not UNSC: no emblem or insignia. Not Xbox: no X, no orb or jewel; the lime is a glow accent shifted to yellow-green, on gunmetal.

07

2001 hardware: translucent jelly in black plastic

Jelly Panel

A window of teal jelly set in chunky black plastic, glowing from inside, with the stencil frosted into it and a gloss across the top: the translucent hardware of 2001 wearing a squad marking.

Why it's safe. A rounded window in a rounded case with our own stencil letters; no device, shape or type from the game or any console.

Why it's not UNSC or Xbox. Not UNSC: no emblem or insignia. Not Xbox: a teal rounded square, not a green X or orb.

08

2001 hardware: brushed chrome badge

Chrome Insignia

A faceted badge in bevelled chrome around a gunmetal field, with an embossed chrome stencil H1, a single rank-style chevron and a teal light line running inside the rim: insignia as 2001 hardware would cast it.

Why it's safe. Our own angular badge outline with generic chevron and stencil letters; no wings, star, eagle, globe or any insignia from the series.

Why it's not UNSC or Xbox. Not UNSC: no eagle, globe or wings-and-star. Not Xbox: chrome and teal, an angular badge, no X or orb.

At small size

Each variant's small version at its true 16 pixels in a light and a dark browser tab, on white and on dark, the one-colour mark at 16 pixels, and the small version enlarged eight times.

Top two

Close behind: Serial Plate is the most practical lockup (the plate is the wordmark), and Chrome Insignia is the most "2001 console" of the badges. Squad Patch and ID Tag are lovely merchandise but busier as a front-page mark.

No. 1

Backlit

It is the brief in one object: a real military stencil, rendered as 2001 console hardware with the light coming through the cut-outs. It is the strongest app icon of the round, the 16-pixel version is a clean lime H1 on gunmetal, and it stays clearly its own mark, with no emblem and no X or orb.

No. 2

Hull Marking

The most believable military sci-fi mark here: it looks like paint on equipment, not a logo pretending to be one. The seams, fasteners and wear carry the world, the stencil alphabet is ours, and it simplifies cleanly to a sand H1 on an olive plate at 16 pixels.
